propositions.text: Claimant is a 27-year-old Nigerian citizen seeking refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXXXX XXXX claims to be a 27-year-old citizen of Nigeria and seeks refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (the Act).

paragraphs.summary: The claimant, a 27-year-old Nigerian citizen, seeks refugee protection under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, as stated by the claimant.

propositions.text: The claimant's Personal Information Form allegations are summarized.
propositions.quote: The allegations in the claimant's Personal Information Form (PIF) can be summarized as follows.

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes the allegations in the claimant's Personal Information Form.

propositions.text: In 1999, claimant was forced into a relationship by her father, lived with a 55-year-old man for one year until his death.
propositions.quote: In 1999, the claimant was forced by her father into a relationship with a 55-year-old man with whom she lived for one year until he passed away from illness.

propositions.text: After his death, his brother insisted claimant marry him and be circumcised; claimant fled to aunt's home, then lived homeless for 5 years.
propositions.quote: After his death, one of his brothers, 69-year-old XXXX, insisted the claimant marry him and that she be circumcised. With no support from her immediate family, the claimant fled to her aunt's home and, after XXXX family found out where she was, to XXXX, where she lived homeless for 5 years.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says her father forced her into a relationship in 1999; after the man's death, his brother forced marriage and circumcision demands led her to flee and live homeless for 5 years.

propositions.text: Claimant survived by begging, met a man who helped her flee Nigeria for 150,000 Nairas, traveled through Accra and Switzerland, then arrived in Canada pregnant in 2008.
propositions.quote: Surviving on begging and with no support or news from her family, she eventually met a man called XXXX who accepted to help her flee the country upon payment of a sum of 150,000 Nairas. On XXXX, the claimant left XXXX for Accra, and then Switzerland where she spent one week before flying to Canada where she landed on XXXX, 2008 and immediately filed a claim for asylum. She was several months pregnant at that time.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says she survived by begging, paid to flee Nigeria, traveled through Accra and Switzerland, and arrived in Canada pregnant in 2008.

propositions.text: Claimant is not a Convention Refugee nor a person in need of protection under the Act, though humanitarian reasons may justify not returning her to Nigeria.
propositions.quote: Although humanitarian and compassionate reasons may justify not returning the claimant to Nigeria, the panel finds that the claimant is not a "Convention Refugee" pursuant to section 96 of the Act nor a "person in need of protection" pursuant to section 97(1) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the claimant is not a Convention Refugee or person in need of protection, though humanitarian reasons may justify not returning her.

propositions.text: The panel followed the Chairperson's Guidelines for Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution in making its determination.
propositions.quote: In making the determination, the panel followed the Chairperson's Guidelines for Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The panel followed the Chairperson's Guidelines for Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution in its determination.

propositions.text: The key issue is whether an internal flight alternative (IFA) exists.
propositions.quote: The claimant having satisfactorily established her identity and general credibility, the determinative issue in this matter is the existence of an internal flight alternative (IFA).

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the existence of an internal flight alternative as the key issue after accepting claimant's identity and credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant failed to prove a serious possibility of persecution or risk of harm everywhere in Nigeria or that seeking refuge elsewhere in Nigeria is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Indeed, the claimant did not meet her burden of establishing on a balance of probabilities that there was a serious possibility of persecution or a probable risk of harm everywhere in Nigeria and that it would be unreasonable for her to seek refuge in another part of her country, namely Lagos.

propositions.text: Failure to prove this is sufficient to dispose of the claim.
propositions.quote: Failure to do so is, in and of itself, sufficient to dispose of her claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant failed to prove persecution risk everywhere or unreasonableness of internal flight, which disposes of her claim.

propositions.text: The panel addresses claimant's arguments why she cannot live safely in the proposed IFA.
propositions.quote: When asked why she could not live safely in the proposed IFA, the claimant raised several arguments, which the panel disposes of as follows: The person who wishes to marry her by force and have her undergo female genital mutilation (FGM) (the Agent) will find and harm her.

paragraphs.summary: The panel addresses claimant's arguments that the Agent would find and harm her in the proposed internal flight alternative.

propositions.text: Though claimant did not initially mention fear of forced FGM, the panel accepts her genuine fear of forced FGM and forced marriage by the Agent.
propositions.quote: Though the claimant did not mention, when she arrived in Canada, a fear of being forced by her Agent to undergo FGM (see the absence of any mention of this in her interview with the immigration agent and question 3 of the immigration form IMM-54743), the panel accepts her testimony - confirming her story as set out in her PIF - that she genuinely harbours such a fear, in addition to her fear of being forced to marry her Agent.

paragraphs.summary: The panel accepts the claimant's genuine fear of forced FGM and forced marriage by the Agent despite initial omission.

propositions.text: The Agent is unlikely to find or harm claimant in Lagos due to age, lack of interest, and legal deterrents against FGM in his state.
propositions.quote: However, the panel finds the Agent would not be interested or capable of locating her in Lagos. To begin with, her Agent, of whom she has received no news since at least 2002, would be approximately 80 years old today if he were still alive. An uneducated XXXX having allegedly "inherited" six other wives upon the death of his younger brother (the claimant's original husband), in addition to having at least one other wife, the Agent's interest in expending the effort of locating the claimant in XXXX and forcefully bringing her back to his village is likely not very high - assuming he even had this capacity. And even if the claimant was considered by tradition the "property" of the Agent's entire family, including his own male offspring, as the documentary evidence4 indicates is the case in other ethnic groups, the fact that the claimant lived in XXXX for a period of over five years without encountering difficulties in regards to this Agent or his family, tends to confirm this lack of capacity or interest on behalf of anyone in her Agent's family who might claim "inheritance" rights against her. Though the claimant is young and apparently healthy, she is uneducated, and as this documentary evidence5 reports, resources are scarce and men no longer want to waste theirs to cater for a woman who do not belong to them legally. Furthermore, the documentary evidence6 also confirms that FGM in XXXX state, where the Agent resides, is a crime punishable by no less than three years and/or a fine. This too is a disincentive to pursuing the claimant further.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the Agent unlikely to locate or harm claimant in Lagos due to his age, lack of interest, claimant's past safety, scarce resources, and FGM criminalization.

propositions.text: Claimant's immediate family never found or bothered her and she does not believe they could find her in Lagos.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the claimant was never found or bothered by her own immediate family members, who allegedly insisted she comply with her Agent's wishes - in part because they were shamed by her behavior, possibly also because the father's debt towards the claimant's first husband might still be owing. The claimant even admitted that she did not think her family could find her in Lagos.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant's immediate family never found or bothered her and she does not believe they could find her in Lagos.

propositions.text: Even if Agent or family could find claimant in Lagos, state protection would be reasonably available and claimant should seek it.
propositions.quote: Regardless, even if her Agent, his family or hers were interested and capable of locating her in Lagos - which the panel doesn't believe, it would still find that state protection would be reasonably forthcoming and that it would be reasonable for the claimant to seek it. In making this finding, the panel acknowledges that some of the documentary evidence7 corroborates the claimant's testimony to the effect that such matters (specifically FGM but likely forced marriage) are considered a private matter and that Nigerian authorities generally do not interfere. One quoted source, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) in Nigeria, an independent government agency, reported more specifically that the "traditional attitude" of a police officer or a village council would normally determine their level of concern and intervention in any given case.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds that even if the Agent or family could find claimant in Lagos, state protection would be reasonably available and claimant should seek it.

propositions.text: More recent evidence shows NHRC offers mediation, legal assistance, and protection against FGM; federal government opposes FGM and provides some protection.
propositions.quote: The panel however prefers the more recent documentary evidence.8 It reports the same NHRC as stating at a later date that resorting to its services is a real possibility, both for women and for parents of girls facing pressure from the extended family to have FGM performed on themselves or their children. In such situations, the commission can mediate or offer legal assistance - including bringing cases to court.9 It further confirms that the law criminalizes the removal of any part of a sexual organ from a woman or girl, except for medical reasons approved by a doctor, and provides for a fine of 50,000 naira (approximately $332), one year's imprisonment, or both for a first offense and doubled penalties for a second conviction. Though it has yet to take legal action to curb the practice, the federal government publicly opposes FGM and is making efforts in providing protection to women fleeing domestic violence, FGM or forced marriage. Sources on the ground confirm that the protection is weak, but it is progressing. Not only is the Federal Ministry of Women's Affairs and Social Development providing shelter and legal assistance to women who are victims of violence, FGM or forced marriage, the police as well are developing more gender awareness and receiving training to better handle such cases. Gender Desks have been established in Lagos and Abuja, and more are in the process of being established. The police officers employed in these Gender Desks have received special training on gender-based violence and women who approach one of these will definitely be assisted. One UN representative confirms that the NHRC is functioning well and offers free legal assistance and facilitates necessary physical protection of women who are victims of domestic violence, FGM or forced marriage. They added that there are many women, including many victims of domestic violence, forced marriages and FGM, who have turned to the government for help and they have been assisted. Finally, a third on-the-ground source confirms that the Nigerian authorities are involved in the combat against FGM practices and that a woman who tries to escape FGM will be able to seek assistance and be protected by the authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The panel prefers recent evidence showing NHRC offers mediation, legal help, and protection against FGM; government opposes FGM and provides some protection.

propositions.text: Claimant must prove state protection is unavailable to be a Convention refugee or person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: For the claimant to be a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection", she must demonstrate that state protection is not available to her.

propositions.text: Canada's international protection responsibility arises only when national protection is unavailable.
propositions.quote: Canada's responsibility to provide international protection only becomes engaged when national or state protection is unavailable to the claimant.

propositions.text: Claimant must provide clear and convincing proof of state's inability to protect.
propositions.quote: It is well established that it is the responsibility of a claimant to provide persuasive evidence ("clear and convincing proof") of the state's inability to protect the claimant.

propositions.text: Alternative evidence like testimony of women in similar situations may be used to meet the clear and convincing test.
propositions.quote: In cases where the claimant cannot rely on the more standard or typical forms of evidence as "clear and convincing proof" of failure of state protection, reference may need to be made to alternative forms of evidence to meet the "clear and convincing" test, such as the testimony of women in similar situations where there was a failure of state protection, or the testimony of the claimant herself regarding past personal incidents or those of people she knows where state protection did not materialize.

propositions.text: No such evidence was established; panel prefers documentary evidence over claimant's assertion that police protection requires money.
propositions.quote: No such evidence was established and the panel prefers the above-mentioned evidence to the claimant's general assertion that without money, no police protection would be forthcoming.

propositions.text: Panel finds adequate state protection would be available in Lagos, especially with NGO assistance, so claimant would not face persecution or harm there.
propositions.quote: It therefore finds that adequate state protection against her Agent would be available to the claimant if she chose to seek it in Lagos, especially if sought in parallel with the assistance of non governmental organisations (NGOs), like those referred to below, who deal with FGM matters on a regular basis and would more likely than not have the appropriate weight and connections to help the claimant elicit an adequate response from the authorities. Accordingly, the panel finds the claimant would not face a serious possibility of persecution or a probable risk of harm in Lagos in reference to her fear of her Agent.

propositions.text: Claimant argues she has no one to assist her and her daughter, family disowned her, and lack of education worsens her situation.
propositions.quote: The claimant has no one to assist her and her daughter. Her family has disowned her and without their assistance, she is doomed. Her lack of education compounds her difficult situation.

paragraphs.summary: The court states claimant must prove state protection is unavailable; no such evidence was given; adequate protection is available in Lagos with NGO help; claimant says family disowned her and she lacks education.

propositions.text: Claimant says family disowned her for shame; she was homeless and resorted to prostitution; no assistance was received despite begging; unaware of NGOs.
propositions.quote: According to her testimony, her immediate family members will not assist her and have essentially disowned her because of the shame she has brought to them. If returned to Nigeria, she would therefore be helpless and she does not believe anyone will provide assistance. To support this belief, she relates her own experience in XXXX between 2002 and 2008 where she allegedly was forced to essentially live as a homeless person and eventually resort to prostitution to survive. During this time, she would have begged for assistance from strangers in the street, yet was slapped down and afforded none. Though she admits not having contacted any NGOs, by sheer ignorance of their existence, she questions where they were when she was in need. No one came to her, she lamented.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant testifies her family disowned her, she was homeless and resorted to prostitution, received no help, and was unaware of NGOs.

propositions.text: Panel empathizes with claimant's hardships but prefers documentary evidence supporting internal relocation and available assistance.
propositions.quote: The panel empathizes with the claimant and her alleged hardships in XXXX as well as her refusal to acknowledge the availability of assistance. However, it prefers the documentary evidence below which it construes as supporting the view that internal relocation is a viable option for women in the claimant's situation - as long as they seek the available assistance.

paragraphs.summary: The panel empathizes with claimant's hardships but prefers evidence showing internal relocation and assistance are viable options.

propositions.text: Research and consultations show NGOs and religious groups provide shelter, counseling, legal aid, vocational training, and empowerment for relocating women in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: Indeed, recent research and consultation12 with several ostensibly authoritative sources "on the ground", including women's rights groups and independent women's shelter NGOs in Nigeria, recognizes that even without family and social networks, relocation is possible and support services for women are available. Though it paints a grim picture of the reality facing such women, it essentially reports that through religious congregations and NGOs, shelter, counseling, legal assistance, vocational training and post-shelter assistance in the form of empowerment, as well as assistance to find accommodation and/or employment for relocating women, is available. Even the Government has started providing relevant services, albeit in limited quantities in Abuja and for durations of four to five months only, under the Federal Ministry of Women's Affairs and Social Development.

paragraphs.summary: Research shows NGOs and religious groups provide various support services for relocating women in Nigeria, with limited government services.

propositions.text: Panel considers claimant's ability to safely travel to Lagos, noting return flight likely lands there and Nigeria is relatively safe with no prior travel difficulties shown.
propositions.quote: In determining the reasonableness of the claimant's recourse to the proposed IFA, the panel has taken into consideration her ability, because of her gender, to safely travel to Lagos. It notes in this respect that the claimant's return flight from Canada would likely land her directly in Lagos. Even if this were not the case, the panel would still find the claimant is more likely than not able to safely travel within the country considering Nigeria is a relatively safe country as regards crime rates13 and that the claimant did not establish she encountered any difficulties on her earlier bus trips between her village and XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant likely able to safely travel to Lagos, noting flight arrival and Nigeria's relative safety and no prior travel issues.

propositions.text: Panel considers religious, cultural, economic factors; claimant is young, healthy, Christian, likely to find supportive community in Lagos.
propositions.quote: Moreover, in making this determination, the panel also has given due regards to various factors, including religious, cultural and economic factors, that could force the claimant to face undue hardship in staying in Lagos. To begin with, she is a youthful and apparently healthy person -physically and mentally - who has succeeded in establishing herself half-way across the world, far from family and friends. Secondly, though religious tensions exist throughout the country, Lagos is known to host large numbers of both Muslims and Christians.14 In light of the claimant's testimony that she is Christian, the panel finds that the claimant would more likely than not encounter a supportive community in that respect in Lagos.

propositions.text: Claimant's recent conversion might cause ostracism but no evidence shows it would cause persecution or make Lagos unviable as IFA.
propositions.quote: As regards her counsel's observation that the claimant could face problems because she recently converted, the panel acknowledges that in many communities, converts can indeed face ostracism.15 However, the claimant did not allege, let alone establish, how this could pose a problem for her in Lagos, especially where no one knows her. Even accepting she may be frowned upon by Muslims, and possibly socially excluded by them, the panel does not believe, after reviewing the documentary evidence, that this type of treatment could rise to persecution or render Lagos an unviable option as an IFA.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant likely to find a supportive Christian community in Lagos; recent conversion ostracism is unproven and not persecution.

propositions.text: The city is the nation's largest and hosts all ethnic groups according to documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: the city is the nation's largest one, where arguably people migrate from many parts of the country. It consequently also hosts a wide array of ethnic and linguistic groups, to the point that all ethnic groups are represented in the city according to the documentary evidence.

propositions.text: Ethnic affiliation plays a significant role in some rural locations but generally not in internal relocation in large cities like Lagos.
propositions.quote: although ethnic affiliation might play a significant role in some rural locations, notably in regards to job opportunities, it generally does not represent a major issue in connection with internal relocation in the larger cities, such as Lagos.

propositions.text: Support networks are not necessarily limited to certain ethnic groups; Christian and Muslim congregations consider ethnicity irrelevant.
propositions.quote: support networks are not necessarily limited to a certain ethnic group. To wit, Christian and Muslim congregations, recognized as being important networks and sources of assistance in times of need, generally consider the ethnicity of congregation members to be irrelevant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Lagos is the largest city with all ethnic groups, ethnic affiliation is less relevant for relocation, and support networks are ethnically inclusive.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence recognizes Nigerian women face societal discrimination and marginalization despite some improvements.
propositions.quote: the documentary evidence recognizes that Nigerian women face societal discrimination and that they generally remain marginalized, despite some positive improvements, including legislation and the impact of education on breaking down various barriers.

propositions.text: The claimant would be exposed to this discrimination in Lagos.
propositions.quote: The claimant would necessarily be exposed to this reality in Lagos.

propositions.text: It was not alleged or established that this discrimination amounts to persecution or unduly harsh living conditions for the claimant.
propositions.quote: it was not alleged - and even less established - that this discrimination amounts to persecution or that it would render living conditions unduly harsh for the claimant - taken alone or in conjunction with other factors.

propositions.text: This discrimination adds complexity but does not exclude the existence of an internal flight alternative (IFA).
propositions.quote: this reality adds a level of complexity to women living in Nigeria generally, but does not exclude the existence of an IFA in the country.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Nigerian women face discrimination but it is not persecution or harsh enough to exclude an IFA for the claimant in Lagos.

propositions.text: The claimant has limited education and no literacy skills, facing economic constraints and responsibility for her daughter.
propositions.quote: the claimant boasts limited formal education and has no writing or reading skills. She undoubtedly will therefore face a number of economic constraints, compounded by the fact that she is now responsible for her minor daughter.

propositions.text: Nigeria has no welfare system; people rely on immediate and extended family in times of need.
propositions.quote: Nigeria has no welfare system and people mainly rely on their immediate and extended family in times of need and crisis.

propositions.text: The claimant cannot rely on her numerous siblings but could rely on a maternal uncle and an 'auntie' who previously helped her.
propositions.quote: relying on her numerous siblings appears to be impossible... the panel finds the claimant could nonetheless rely on some support from one of her maternal uncles... The same could be said in regards to her "auntie", who provided shelter to her for approximately two years before the claimant fled to XXXX.

propositions.text: The claimant could seek support from a trustworthy friend in XXXX who has helped her before.
propositions.quote: the panel believes the claimant could seek some form of support from her friend in XXXX, who already proved to be trustworthy and a valuable resource to her in the past by offering her shelter as well as a safe location to store her savings.

propositions.text: Many Nigerians establish other support networks beyond family, including religious, political, charitable, and social groups.
propositions.quote: Many Nigerians establish other support networks that may complement or (in some cases) replace the extended family. Examples of such support networks are religious congregations, religious organizations, age grades/sets, political organizations, charities, secret societies and guilds.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant faces economic challenges but has potential support from family, friends, and other Nigerian social networks.

propositions.text: Government and non-governmental organizations provide short- and medium-term assistance to help the claimant and her daughter.
propositions.quote: the various aforementioned government and non-governmental organizations are available, for short-term and medium-term assistance to help sustain herself and her daughter.

propositions.text: The claimant can seek longer-term autonomy through employment matching her skills or training programs.
propositions.quote: seeking longer-term autonomy in the form of an employment commensurate with her present skills (for example, dishwashing in a restaurant or domestic chores) or those she may acquire through the aforementioned training programs offered by various organizations.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds assistance and employment or training opportunities are available to the claimant and her daughter.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence reports 'taking to the streets' is frequent for young women without means, a reality the claimant knows.
propositions.quote: the documentary evidence also reports that "taking to the streets" is unfortunately a frequent scenario for young women or women who do not have the capacity or the means to do otherwise - a reality that the claimant allegedly knows too well.

propositions.text: The claimant's recent experience in Canada and available support services suggest she can avoid such dire scenarios in Lagos or other big cities.
propositions.quote: the panel is of the view that the claimant can avoid such dire scenarios by seeking assistance from the various support services referred to above. This, whether she is in Lagos or in any other big city she may seek to establish herself in to avoid being found.

propositions.text: Sources insist any woman needing assistance in Nigeria can find it if aware of women's groups to contact.
propositions.quote: some sources even insisting that any woman who is in need of assistance and protection in Nigeria will find it, irrespective of where she may be in the country, as long as she is aware of a women's group she can contact.

propositions.text: The claimant's skepticism is based on her experience living under a bridge with no assistance, but recent experiences and organizations like LACVAW increase likelihood of assistance.
propositions.quote: It appreciates the claimant's scepticism in this respect, based essentially on her own experiences living under a bridge. As she explained, no one came and offered her assistance. However, with the benefit of her recent experiences, and through hotlines and organizations like LACVAW... being able to contact such an organization - and find assistance - is highly likely.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that despite past hardships, the claimant can likely access support services in Lagos or other cities to avoid dire situations.

propositions.text: Relocation will be challenging and harsh but this does not rule out an internal flight alternative (IFA).
propositions.quote: the panel recognizes that the relocation will have its challenges and likely be a very difficult, even harsh experience. However, this does not suffice to rule out an IFA.

propositions.text: The threshold to establish an IFA is unreasonable is very high, requiring conditions jeopardizing life and safety.
propositions.quote: the threshold the claimant must meet to establish that an IFA is unreasonable is a very high one, requiring nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize her life and safety.

propositions.text: The claimant has not met the test; Lagos is a realistic IFA that likely would not jeopardize her life and safety.
propositions.quote: the panel finds that the claimant has not met this test... Lagos as an IFA is a realistic option for the claimant in her particular circumstances, one that would likely not jeopardize her life and safety.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the claimant has not shown Lagos is an unreasonable IFA and it likely would not jeopardize her life or safety.

propositions.text: The claimant is not a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection under the Act.
propositions.quote: the panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" within the meaning of section 96 of the Act, nor is she a "person in need of protection" with respect to section 97(1)(a) and (b) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection under the Act.
